DeepSeek's Harness team said in an article published on Saturday that its experimental "super-agent" architecture is designed to allow AI to continuously monitor information, manage multiple tasks in parallel and take action with less human supervision. The development points to a broader shift in China's fast-moving AI industry, where competition is increasingly moving beyond model size and benchmark scores toward agents that can plan, execute and complete real-world work. As AI models become better at handling individual tasks, Deep-Seek said the bottleneck is increasingly human attention: users still have to switch between different conversations, keep track of their progress and provide instructions. The super-agent approach is intended to move much of that coordination into the AI system itself, allowing people to focus more on higher-level decisions and reviewing results rather than overseeing each step of a task. Deep-Seek stressed that the architecture remains an engineering exploration rather than a feature available in its existing products. highlights.content: [![](https://gritdaily.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/07/Screenshot_2025-10-21_at_2.23.29_AM-removebg-preview.png)](https://gritdaily.com) [![](https://gritdaily.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/07/Screenshot_2025-10-21_at_2.23.29_AM-removebg-preview.png)](https://gritdaily.com) # TokenPulse: Building the Leadership Team Behind Cost-Efficient AI Inference By [John Boitnott](https://gritdaily.com/author/jboitnott/) [John Boitnott](https://gritdaily.com/author/jboitnott/) has been verified by Muck Rack's editorial team ![](https://gritdaily.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/image1-3-768x432.jpg) Image Source: TokenPulse [#Artificial Intelligence](https://gritdaily.com/category/artificial-intelligence) / share Published on November 2, 2026 As artificial intelligence (AI) moves from model training into large-scale production, inference computing is becoming an increasingly important factor in the economics of AI infrastructure. Inference demand is climbing alongside the global AI infrastructure market, which is projected to grow [from $982 billion in 2025 to $1.98 trillion by 2027](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2026-09-16-gartner-forecasts-worldwide-ai-spending-to-grow-49-point-5-percent-in-2026), doubling in size over the two-year period. Companies deploying AI applications face rising inference costs, demanding real-time latency requirements, and the challenge of scaling their platforms as traffic grows. In this environment, access to GPUs alone is no longer sufficient. The more difficult task is turning available computing capacity into reliable, cost-efficient token output at scale. Doing so requires not only advanced hardware and software optimization, but also the infrastructure partnerships, operational expertise, and commercial relationships needed to support growing demand. This is the challenge that [TokenPulse](http://www.tokenpulse.com/), a next-generation AI inference infrastructure company headquartered in San Francisco and Singapore, is seeking to address. Following the opening of its Asia-Pacific Operating Hub in Singapore, the company is bringing together data-center resources, GPU infrastructure, optimized inference engines, and globally coordinated serving capabilities to support AI workloads across regions. Beyond its technology strategy, TokenPulse is placing considerable emphasis on the leadership team responsible for putting that infrastructure into operation. With backgrounds spanning data centers, government, investment, cloud engineering, and enterprise commercialization, its executives bring different capabilities to the increasingly complex business of AI inference. ## Infrastructure Leadership and Regional Delivery At the center of TokenPulse’s infrastructure strategy is Chairman Thomas Pang, whose more than 30 years of executive experience span government, investment, infrastructure, and corporate leadership. Pang spent over two decades with Keppel, including serving as CEO of Keppel’s Data Centres & Networks Division from 2014 to 2024. In that role, he oversaw the group’s global data-center portfolio and digital connectivity businesses, gaining experience in the infrastructure development and partnerships that underpin large-scale computing operations. That background is particularly relevant as TokenPulse expands its presence in Southeast Asia. While GPU performance and software efficiency remain central to AI inference, the ability to secure suitable data-center capacity, coordinate regional infrastructure resources, and establish long-term partnerships can be equally important to commercial delivery. From its Singapore operating hub, TokenPulse is developing infrastructure relationships across Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand, and the wider region. Singapore also serves as a strategic link between North America’s AI technology and customer ecosystems and Southeast Asia’s expanding data-center and energy resources. Essentially, the performance of these models increasingly depends less on the compute capability of a processor – how fast the chip can calculate – and more on how quickly the chip can feed data to the calculation. Qualcomm outlined two strategies that are widely used – one that houses the AI model in fast on-chip memory, and another that uses stacked high-bandwidth memory (HBM) to support a processor. highlights.content: # Ebix Launches AI Agent Governance Offering for Regulated Industries ![](https://www.citybiz.co/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/Ebix.jpg) [Ebix](https://edge.prnewswire.com/c/link/?t=0&l=en&o=4810292-1&h=1259667856&u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.ebix.com%2F&a=Ebix) today announced the launch of a new agentic AI security and governance offering for regulated industries through its design and delivery partnership with [intentyx](https://edge.prnewswire.com/c/link/?t=0&l=en&o=4810292-1&h=2137011550&u=https%3A%2F%2Fintentyx.ai%2F&a=intentyx). The offering is built around SMARE (Synthetic Mind Aware Risk Engine), a behavioral security and governance platform for discovering enterprise AI agents, establishing accountability and detecting when agent behavior moves outside its approved business purpose or security boundaries. Ebix will bring [SMARE](https://edge.prnewswire.com/c/link/?t=0&l=en&o=4810292-1&h=485969521&u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.ebix.com%2Fsolutions%2Febixone%2Fresponsible-ai%2F&a=SMARE) to clients across insurance, financial services, healthcare and other regulated industries, combining the technology with Ebix’s industry knowledge, enterprise integration experience, and growing expertise in deploying and governing AI agents within its own environment. As AI agents increasingly access data, use tools, make decisions, and take actions across business systems, traditional security controls address only part of the problem. An agent may have valid credentials and permission to use a system while still taking a sequence of actions that the business never intended. For regulated enterprises, that creates a new control requirement: organizations need visibility not only into what an agent is allowed to do, but what it is actually doing. The market around this problem is developing rapidly. Recent events are already demonstrating the urgency: major U.S. banks have reportedly detected unauthorized third-party AI agents operating inside customer accounts, with some agents attempting actions beyond explicit user instructions, prompting banks to tighten controls around agent access. Regulators are also increasing their focus on agentic AI, including stronger calls for human oversight and controls as autonomous agents move into critical financial and enterprise systems. **How SMARE works** The platform combines available evidence from AI platforms, business applications, cloud environments, identity systems, and existing security tools to create a connected view of agent activity. That activity is evaluated against enterprise security policies and each agent’s approved Design Intent, which defines its purpose, expected actions, authorized tools and data boundaries. SMARE can identify policy violations, unusual behavior and behavioral drift, while preserving the evidence required by security, compliance and operations teams. The enterprise platform is designed to work alongside existing identity, security, and monitoring infrastructure, adding a control layer specifically around AI. “We believe agent governance and behavioral security will become a major enterprise security category in 2027 and beyond,” said [Gagan Sethi](https://www.linkedin.com/in/gagan-sethi/), CEO of Ebix Technologies. “Ebix is entering this market with technology already running in our own environment, deep expertise across AI for regulated industries and an established global client base. We see this developing into a meaningful new opportunity for Ebix as enterprise adoption of AI agents accelerates.” “As enterprises give AI agents access to more applications, data and tools, security teams have a major challenge to understand AI activities as well as access,” said [Nitin Supekar](https://www.linkedin.com/in/nitin-supekar-748702/), founder of intentyx. “SMARE was built to provide that visibility and the evidence required to investigate when behavior moves outside approved intent.” SMARE is commercially available now through Ebix and intentyx and can be deployed as SaaS or within ...

highlights.content: ChannelLife UK - Industry insider news for technology resellers [![ChannelLife UK logo](/brands/cl-new-logo.svg) United Kingdom](/) [Powered By ![TechDay logo](/brands/td-new-logo-right.svg)](https://techday.co.uk) ![Adobe launches free tools for startups in new scheme](https://channellife.co.uk/uploads/story/2026/11/03/startup-founders-desk-laptop-marketing-app-panels-story-323225.webp) [GenAI](https://channellife.co.uk/tag/generative-ai) [AI](https://channellife.co.uk/tag/artificial-intelligence) [Social Media](https://channellife.co.uk/tag/social-media) # Adobe launches free tools for startups in new scheme Tue, 3rd Nov 2026 (Today) [![Mara Sugue](https://channellife.co.uk/rails/active_storage/representations/redirect/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsiZGF0YSI6MTg1OSwicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--c35d782a2ad379dbb3ebd1d7a0269b918cf68f7f/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsiZGF0YSI6eyJmb3JtYXQiOiJ3ZWJwIiwicmVzaXplX3RvX2ZpbGwiOlsxNjAsMTYwXSwicXVhbGl0eSI6ODV9LCJwdXIiOiJ2YXJpYXRpb24ifX0=--89ddf5e6765c65a563c2258053e9d33c05d195da/maraheadshot.webp) MARA SUGUE News Editor](/author/mara-sugue) Adobe has launched Adobe for Startups, a programme offering eligible early-stage companies a year of free access to a package of Adobe and Semrush tools. The scheme targets startups founded within the past five years that have raised less than USD $15 million. Participants will receive 12 months of free access to Firefly Pro Plus, Acrobat Studio, which includes Adobe Express Premium, and Semrush. Adobe is positioning the offer around branding, content creation and customer acquisition at a stage when founders are often handling design, marketing and sales themselves. Alongside software access, the programme includes workshops and other opportunities to learn from Adobe specialists and connect with other founders. **What is included** Firefly Pro Plus is Adobe's generative AI product for image, video and audio work. Acrobat Studio combines PDF tools, Adobe's AI Assistant and Adobe Express, while Semrush adds search and marketing data intended to show how a business appears online across both conventional and AI-led search. The package is designed to bring together content creation, document tools and marketing support in one programme for small teams. Adobe serves a wide range of customers, from individual creators and small businesses to large corporate users. The launch comes as software groups seek to embed AI more deeply into products aimed at smaller businesses and startup teams, which often work with limited budgets and staff. For early-stage companies, branding and customer communication can be difficult to prioritise when product development and fundraising take precedence. **Startup examples** Adobe highlighted several startup users as examples of the businesses it wants to reach through the programme. DataCurve, which works on fan identity and intelligence for sports, media and entertainment organisations, already uses Firefly for creative work and sees broader potential for Adobe tools in linking customer data with content creation. "Creativity is far more powerful when you understand who you're creating for. We already use Adobe Firefly for creative assets, and we see an even bigger opportunity to bring DataCurve's fan intelligence directly into the creative process. Imagine a global soccer club creating content that evolves throughout the season as it learns more about what each fan cares about. Adobe for Startups gives us the tools to start bringing that vision to life," said Aman Johar, Co-founder and CEO of DataCurve. [Editors](https://sciencex.com/help/editorial-team/) have highlighted the following attributes while ensuring the content's credibility: fact-checked preprint trusted source proofread ![KAIST cuts AI fine-tuning from 10 hours to 3… faster development of medical and coding AI](https://scx1.b-cdn.net/csz/news/800a/2026/kaist-cuts-ai-fine-tun.jpg "Conceptual diagram of the clustering-based balanced data sampling and allocation method developed by the research team. Different colors represent clusters of data that have similar effects on learning, and different shapes within the same color represent specific data types within each cluster. In conventional training on the full data set, data types with a large number of samples can be repeatedly included across multiple GPUs, so similar computations may be repeated. The proposed method selects diverse data from each cluster in a balanced way and allocates different clusters to each GPU, which reduces redundant computation. Credit: KAIST") Can AI fine-tuning that once took 10 hours be completed in just three hours? KAIST researchers have developed a technology that selects the most useful training data and distributes it evenly across multiple GPUs. By reducing repetitive learning of similar data, the method shortened training time by up to 69.6% while maintaining nearly the same AI performance. The technology is expected to help develop AI tailored to specific tasks, such as corporate customer service or assisting medical professionals with information retrieval, more quickly and at lower cost. A research team led by professor Jae-Gil Lee from the School of Computing developed "CluSTER," a large language model fine-tuning technology that groups and selects data with similar effects on learning and distributes them evenly across multiple GPUs. The research findings were presented in October 2026 at the Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP 2026) and are available on the *arXiv* preprint server. Hyunjin Kim, a doctoral student in the KAIST School of Computing, participated in the [study](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2609.12584) as the first author, with Lee as the corresponding author. Youngeun Nam, a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Toronto, and Jaemin Han and Wonhyeok Choi, master's students at the KAIST Graduate School of Data Science, participated as co-authors. ## Random allocation repeats similar learning A large language model must be trained further on relevant data before it can be used in a specific field such as coding or medicine. This process is called "fine-tuning." The offering is built around SMARE (Synthetic Mind Aware Risk Engine), a behavioral security and governance platform for discovering enterprise AI agents, establishing accountability and detecting when agent behavior moves outside its approved business purpose or security boundaries. Ebix will bring [SMARE](https://edge.prnewswire.com/c/link/?t=0&l=en&o=4810292-1&h=485969521&u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.ebix.com%2Fsolutions%2Febixone%2Fresponsible-ai%2F&a=SMARE) to clients across insurance, financial services, healthcare and other regulated industries, combining the technology with Ebix’s industry knowledge, enterprise integration experience, and growing expertise in deploying and governing AI agents within its own environment. As AI agents increasingly access data, use tools, make decisions, and take actions across business systems, traditional security controls address only part of the problem. An agent may have valid credentials and permission to use a system while still taking a sequence of actions that the business never intended. For regulated enterprises, that creates a new control requirement: organizations need visibility not only into what an agent is allowed to do, but what it is actually doing. The market around this problem is developing rapidly. Recent events are already demonstrating the urgency: major U.S. banks have reportedly detected unauthorized third-party AI agents operating inside customer accounts, with some agents attempting actions beyond explicit user instructions, prompting banks to tighten controls around agent access. Regulators are also increasing their focus on agentic AI, including stronger calls for human oversight and controls as autonomous agents move into critical financial and enterprise systems. **How SMARE works** The platform combines available evidence from AI platforms, business applications, cloud environments, identity systems, and existing security tools to create a connected view of agent activity. That activity is evaluated against enterprise security policies and each agent’s approved Design Intent, which defines its purpose, expected actions, authorized tools and data boundaries. SMARE can identify policy violations, unusual behavior and behavioral drift, while preserving the evidence required by security, compliance and operations teams. The enterprise platform is designed to work alongside existing identity, security, and monitoring infrastructure, adding a control layer specifically around AI. “We believe agent governance and behavioral security will become a major enterprise security category in 2027 and beyond,” said [Gagan Sethi](https://www.linkedin.com/in/gagan-sethi/), CEO of Ebix Technologies. “Ebix is entering this market with technology already running in our own environment, deep expertise across AI for regulated industries and an established global client base. AI Agents.content: # When AI agents agree on the data but not what it means Presented by SAP Enterprise AI agents that share the same data can still make conflicting decisions because raw data rarely captures the business context — the processes, policies and priorities that determine what that data means to the company. As agents take on more decision-making, those gaps in context become harder to contain. Three problems emerge when multiple agents act without shared business semantics: identical figures lead different functions to different conclusions, agents that work correctly on their own combine into the wrong outcome, and accuracy degrades as data accumulates. Enterprises have spent years loading ever more records into central data platforms, separating them in the process from the policies, processes and business context where they originated. That separation is at the root of the problem, says Irfan Khan, president and chief product officer for SAP Data & Analytics. “If you access data from a source environment and it doesn’t have the context, the likelihood is you’re going to make an ill-informed decision,” he explains. "Users learn from history only when institutional knowledge helps them separate signal from noise. An agent starts with no such knowledge unless the company supplies it." ## The agent coordination gap in multi-agent AI systems Traditional data strategies extract records from source systems and centralize them, which separates the data from the semantics and process context it carried at the source. The shift toward separating storage and compute let companies scale each independently and encouraged many to build multiple data lakes alongside on-premises estates, flat files and object stores, leading to fragmented data increasingly separated from its original business context. In multi-agent systems, missing context doesn’t stay a data problem. Once agents divide a business process among them, it becomes a coordination failure. For instance, a procurement agent negotiates longer payment terms to improve margins, a treasury agent delays payments to preserve liquidity, and a compliance agent holds payments until every validation clears. Each one is performing its assigned job correctly, but together they're stalling supplier payments long enough that critical vendors start deprioritizing the company, and no internal system flags anything as broken. Plus, few business processes run on a single agent from end to end. An order entry agent might hand off to one that checks inventory, which hands off to another that files a procurement request or decrements stock. If those steps run out of sequence, one agent can decrement an account before another has confirmed the goods exist, and the task can be completed, but the outcome can still be wrong. And there's no reason agents would coordinate any better than people do when nobody manages the handoffs, Khan says. “It’s almost like pushing out a task to 20 individual people to go and get it done for a client, and then you realize that nobody held a team meeting,” he says. “Nobody kept an inventory of where you were, or where you are within the process.” ## A business data fabric gives agents shared business context Giving agents access to distributed enterprise data solves only part of the problem. They also need a common understanding of how the business expects that data to be interpreted and acted upon. It connects data and its semantics with the processes, policies, and other business knowledge that govern how the data is used, while allowing agents to reach information across distributed environments. AI Agents.content: By Manish Sood, founder & CEO of Reltio, an SAP company, and Irfan Khan, president & chief product officer of SAP Data & Analytics Sixty-three percent of organizations either lack or aren't sure they have the data management required for AI, according to Gartner. Worse, the firm predicts that companies will abandon 60% of AI projects by the end of this year due to a lack of AI-ready data. Not because of model performance, talent, or cost. It's the data they already have but can't use. Across every industry, enterprises are deploying autonomous AI agents to execute workflows and make decisions at machine speed. Yet the data those agents rely on remains fragmented, duplicated, and inconsistent. The agent isn't the bottleneck — the scattered data layer underneath it is. Before AI agents can deliver meaningful ROI, organizations must bridge the gap between content and context. Otherwise, they risk automating ambiguity at unprecedented speed. Ask a large organization how many active customers it has, and sales, finance, and support will each cite a different number. None of them is necessarily wrong. They simply never agreed on what "active" means in the first place. When a human employee spots a data discrepancy, they ask a colleague for context. An AI agent does not. Unless explicitly programmed to flag ambiguity, an agent will instantly select an answer and act on it across enterprise systems. That speed makes agents valuable, but also dangerous. An agent acting on an incorrect definition of "active customer" doesn't just produce a flawed spreadsheet; it triggers misrouted shipments, duplicate outreach campaigns, or unnecessary compliance flags. The errors compound before human oversight can intervene. The consequences of bad data aren't new, but the speed at which they now play out is. When this problem surfaces, the typical executive instinct is to consolidate and move everything into a single data lake or platform. But consolidation merely puts conflicting records in the same room. It doesn't resolve which record is accurate, how the records relate, or what "active customer" means in a specific workflow. Consolidation gathers data in one place. Unification resolves identity, establishes shared definitions, maps relationships across systems, and encodes the business rules governing what an agent is permitted to do. Without that contextual layer, there is no single source of truth — only a larger warehouse of conflicting data, and an AI agent with the keys to act on it. Consider an AI agent tasked with resolving a delayed customer order. To complete the task, it must: To choose the right action, the agent needs a current, unified view of the customer, order, and related records, along with the business rules that govern its response. Delivering that context requires a real-time, unified data product. This is an ongoing discipline, not a one-time cleanup: Identities, relationships, and rules must stay current as records change and new information arrives. Giving agents relevant, reconciled context can also reduce token consumption by limiting the need to retrieve and compare conflicting records. Forrester's research identifies context management and error recovery as sources of AI agent failure, underscoring that fixes focused on prompts or model tuning are insufficient. Enterprises must address the quality and reliability of the context their agents use to act. They must also break down the wall between analytical and operational data. Autonomous agents need to reason across historical patterns and real-time operational state simultaneously, without sacrificing governance or speed. The foundational models powering AI agents will continue to commoditize. Within a few years, the raw model capabilities available to competing enterprises will look virtually identical. AI Agents.content: # The agentic web is here With the rise of personal AI assistants, the internet isn't just for humans anymore. In 2001, a decade after he invented the World Wide Web, Tim Berners-Lee articulated a new vision. Together with two colleagues, he published an article in the magazine Scientific American in which he outlined what he called the “Semantic Web”: an internet designed to be navigated by autonomous software agents that could address our every need, without requiring us to muck about with browsers and search engines ourselves. To illustrate what this might look like, Berners-Lee and his colleagues told a story about a pair of siblings who use their agents to automatically research and book a physical therapy appointment for their mother, making sure it would be covered by insurance and fit their busy calendars. At the turn of the millennium, this vision seemed far-fetched: Google had only been online for a couple of years, and most people were still on dial-up connections. But a quarter-century on, the dream of autonomous software agents that use the internet and carry out tasks for us has finally been realized. New tools such as Meta’s blockbuster Muse agent and OpenAI’s Dots are logging record downloads and being given access to people’s bank accounts and email inboxes, and Anthropic launched a research preview of its own Claude Duet agent in October. And in a worrying incident, agents created by OpenAI broke free of their badly protected sandbox and caused havoc on the open web. Just as the rise of smartphones sparked the development of a more atomized and attention-grabbing internet, the advent of powerful AI systems heralds a new era: We’re facing not the semantic web but the agentic web. This new web is developing out of sight and in ways that might not be entirely within our control. As it grows, the agentic web will inevitably transform the human web—and whether the human web survives this transition is anyone’s guess. For Berners-Lee’s original vision to work, internet users would have had to annotate the pages they built with special tags so that a software agent could understand each element’s meaning—say, “street address” for the part of a physical therapy office’s web page that indicates its location and “appointment types” for the list of services. And so the idea never really caught on. “It’s a lot of labor,” says Eni Mustafaraj, an associate professor of computer science at Wellesley College. “And the benefits of that were not obvious.” For the next two decades, then, the internet remained a place for humans that put humans first, with the odd Twitter reply bot or web scraper to round things out. Large language models changed that. Unlike the agents that Berners-Lee was imagining, today’s LLM-based agents don’t need any tags to understand which part of the text on a clinic’s site is its address and which details the services it offers. They can search for and process text far faster than any human, and agents with multimodal capabilities can even interpret screenshots of websites and click on specific elements such as hyperlinks and drop-down menus. They’re also just a way more intuitive means of finding information and accomplishing tasks online. Rather than poring over pages of Google results to find a budget-friendly product dupe or a half-remembered meme, why not have Claude or ChatGPT peruse hundreds of sites in just a few seconds, guided only by your vague query? Or go one step further and use a personal assistant agent like Muse to hunt down a restaurant reservation or book a flight. As agents flood online spaces, this new user base is changing the web for good. Time magazine, for instance, is publishing versions of its articles that are easier for agents to parse and has started selling ads targeted at them. AI Agents.content: [Infosecurity Magazine Home](https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/) » [Opinions](https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/opinions/) » [You Are Not the Target of AI Agents: You Are the Shortcut](https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/opinions/target-ai-agents-shortcut/) # You Are Not the Target of AI Agents: You Are the Shortcut [Opinion](https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/opinions/) ## Written by ![Photo of Donavan Cheah](https://assets.infosecurity-magazine.com/s3/infosec-media/images/profile/d6ec688c-4a91-4391-a191-e961a10a18f9.jpg?width=64&height=64&mode=crop&scale=both&format=webp) ### [Donavan Cheah](https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/profile/donavan-cheah/) Emerging Trends Working Group Member, ISACA During an internal cyber-capability evaluation, an autonomous AI agent driven by a combination of [OpenAI](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/07/22/open-ai-cyber-models-hack-hugging-face.html) models escaped a constrained environment and [compromised Hugging Face](https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/openai-hugging-face-warning-shot/) while seeking [ExploitGym](https://openai.com/index/hugging-face-model-evaluation-security-incident/) solutions. Investigators believe the agent selected Hugging Face not as an ultimate target, but because it might hold information useful to completing the benchmark. Hugging Face was not merely valuable in itself. It was useful as a shortcut. Because of this, CISOs need to view risk differently. Hugging Face was the victim of reward hacking behavior by AI agents. ## **What is Reward Hacking?** Reward-hacking-like evaluation gaming occurs when a system pursues the measured outcome through a method the designer did not intend. In the AI agent context, this refers to AI agents [cheating](https://www.aisi.gov.uk/blog/cheating-behaviour-in-frontier-model-evaluations) on their tasks, which the UK’s AI Security Institute (AISI) opines makes it difficult for third party evaluators to verify if AI agents behave as they should. One such risk is unintended hacking, especially if the task satisfies the following conditions: * The intended task is difficult or impossible, disincentivizing honest completion * Task success is defined only by the final answer, so it does not matter what the means of obtaining success is * The agent team has broad capabilities, which means that a wide spectrum of tools allows for agent teams to brute force, or enumerate many different tool combinations to perform work, even if not intended * Harms to others are externalities but are not factored into the criteria of evaluation for actions to be taken Therein lie two lessons: * Agent teams may design poor solutions that could result in unsanctioned autonomous action against external systems * Agent teams could inadvertently hack targets that look like the path of least resistance for agent objectives and sub-objectives, which can include all kinds of data depending on the use case ## **Out of Scope Attacks** In 2025, Model Evaluation & Threat Research (METR) illustrated how AI systems [cheat on tasks](https://metr.org/blog/2025-06-05-recent-reward-hacking/#introduction) in an attempt to optimize their test scores. METR observed that AI models can cheat by exploiting bugs. Research done by METR also showed that prompting a model [not to perform reward hacking](https://metr.org/blog/2025-06-05-recent-reward-hacking/) had negligible effect. But this may not be surprising. In the same METR study, they also hypothesized how the usage of reinforcement learning techniques encourages reward hacking, and reward hacking becomes harder to detect even on algorithmically checkable tasks due to the need for subject matter expertise to judge the AI systems. Other examples of reward hacking include the [deletion of failed test cases](https://arxiv.org/html/2606.08960v1), [overwriting the code base to fix a bug](https://arxiv.org/html/2603.02297v1) and [cheating agent benchmarks](https://debugml.github.io/cheating-agents/). Investigators believe the agent selected Hugging Face not as an ultimate target, but because it might hold information useful to completing the benchmark. Hugging Face was not merely valuable in itself. It was useful as a shortcut. Because of this, CISOs need to view risk differently. Hugging Face was the victim of reward hacking behavior by AI agents. ## **What is Reward Hacking?** Reward-hacking-like evaluation gaming occurs when a system pursues the measured outcome through a method the designer did not intend. In the AI agent context, this refers to AI agents [cheating](https://www.aisi.gov.uk/blog/cheating-behaviour-in-frontier-model-evaluations) on their tasks, which the UK’s AI Security Institute (AISI) opines makes it difficult for third party evaluators to verify if AI agents behave as they should. One such risk is unintended hacking, especially if the task satisfies the following conditions: * The intended task is difficult or impossible, disincentivizing honest completion * Task success is defined only by the final answer, so it does not matter what the means of obtaining success is * The agent team has broad capabilities, which means that a wide spectrum of tools allows for agent teams to brute force, or enumerate many different tool combinations to perform work, even if not intended * Harms to others are externalities but are not factored into the criteria of evaluation for actions to be taken Therein lie two lessons: * Agent teams may design poor solutions that could result in unsanctioned autonomous action against external systems * Agent teams could inadvertently hack targets that look like the path of least resistance for agent objectives and sub-objectives, which can include all kinds of data depending on the use case ## **Out of Scope Attacks** In 2025, Model Evaluation & Threat Research (METR) illustrated how AI systems [cheat on tasks](https://metr.org/blog/2025-06-05-recent-reward-hacking/#introduction) in an attempt to optimize their test scores. METR observed that AI models can cheat by exploiting bugs. Research done by METR also showed that prompting a model [not to perform reward hacking](https://metr.org/blog/2025-06-05-recent-reward-hacking/) had negligible effect. But this may not be surprising. In the same METR study, they also hypothesized how the usage of reinforcement learning techniques encourages reward hacking, and reward hacking becomes harder to detect even on algorithmically checkable tasks due to the need for subject matter expertise to judge the AI systems. [Editors](https://sciencex.com/help/editorial-team/) have highlighted the following attributes while ensuring the content's credibility: fact-checked preprint trusted source proofread ![KAIST cuts AI fine-tuning from 10 hours to 3… faster development of medical and coding AI](https://scx1.b-cdn.net/csz/news/800a/2026/kaist-cuts-ai-fine-tun.jpg "Conceptual diagram of the clustering-based balanced data sampling and allocation method developed by the research team. Different colors represent clusters of data that have similar effects on learning, and different shapes within the same color represent specific data types within each cluster. In conventional training on the full data set, data types with a large number of samples can be repeatedly included across multiple GPUs, so similar computations may be repeated. The proposed method selects diverse data from each cluster in a balanced way and allocates different clusters to each GPU, which reduces redundant computation. Credit: KAIST") Can AI fine-tuning that once took 10 hours be completed in just three hours? KAIST researchers have developed a technology that selects the most useful training data and distributes it evenly across multiple GPUs. By reducing repetitive learning of similar data, the method shortened training time by up to 69.6% while maintaining nearly the same AI performance. The technology is expected to help develop AI tailored to specific tasks, such as corporate customer service or assisting medical professionals with information retrieval, more quickly and at lower cost. A research team led by professor Jae-Gil Lee from the School of Computing developed "CluSTER," a large language model fine-tuning technology that groups and selects data with similar effects on learning and distributes them evenly across multiple GPUs. The research findings were presented in October 2026 at the Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP 2026) and are available on the *arXiv* preprint server. Hyunjin Kim, a doctoral student in the KAIST School of Computing, participated in the [study](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2609.12584) as the first author, with Lee as the corresponding author. Youngeun Nam, a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Toronto, and Jaemin Han and Wonhyeok Choi, master's students at the KAIST Graduate School of Data Science, participated as co-authors. ## Random allocation repeats similar learning A large language model must be trained further on relevant data before it can be used in a specific field such as coding or medicine. This process is called "fine-tuning." It is similar to teaching a broadly knowledgeable AI coding problems and solutions or medical questions and answers so that it can perform tasks in that particular field more effectively. This process requires substantial computation, so multiple GPUs divide the data and process it in parallel. The model has also secured first-place rankings on three major embodied AI benchmarks—RoboDojo, RoboTwin and RoboColiseum—and will be fully open-sourced by the end of 2026. GO-3 Preview ranks first on three major embodied AI benchmarks: RoboDojo, RoboTwin and RoboColiseum Built on AGIBOT's proprietary embodied-native architecture, WRAM (World Reasoning Action Model), GO-3 Preview unifies task understanding, future-state prediction and action generation to enable robots to generalize across tasks and perform precise manipulation. Together with Genie Evolver, AGIBOT's hybrid post-training system, and Genie Master, its embodied agent framework, GO-3 Preview forms an integrated learning system spanning pre-training, post-training and real-world deployment. AGIBOT calls this approach "full-lifecycle scaling," designed to help robots develop general capabilities, refine their skills through interaction and continuously improve by learning from real-world work. Large language models have made remarkable advances in reasoning and knowledge-based tasks, but working in the physical world requires more than understanding instructions. Tasks such as grasping small objects and assembling components demand the ability to anticipate environmental changes, manage contact forces and execute precise physical movements. For embodied AI, the challenge is not simply to scale model training, but to extend learning across the entire lifecycle. Rather than developing capabilities solely during pre-training, robots must also learn through post-training interactions and continue adapting after deployment. GO-3 Preview is designed around this principle: enabling robots not only to learn how to perform tasks, but also to become more capable through performing them. **Pre-Training Scaling: Building General Capabilities That Transfer Across Tasks** Consider a simple instruction: "Pick up the cup." The object could be a mug with a handle or a smooth glass, positioned in the middle of a table or surrounded by clutter. To handle such variations, a robot cannot simply memorize specific objects or fixed movements. It needs general-purpose capabilities that transfer across tasks and environments. During pre-training, GO-3 Preview addresses this challenge by scaling both data and model capabilities through its embodied-native WRAM architecture. This approach is designed to help robots learn transferable skills and adapt more quickly to unfamiliar situations. WRAM connects task understanding, future-state prediction and action generation within a unified architecture. LLMs.content: [SHATERED](https://shattered.io/) # Open-Weight AI Models Side by Side: The Spec Sheet ![Dr. Heinrich Vogel](https://shattered.io/wp-content/uploads/avatars/hvogel.webp) [Dr. Heinrich Vogel](https://shattered.io/author/hvogel/) Updated Nov 3, 2026 · 28 min read Five open-weight flagships now compete for the same developer budget, and none of them is the obvious pick. Kimi K3, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, Qwen3.8, GLM-5.3 and Mistral Large 4 all ship weights or have promised them, yet they differ sharply on licence terms, hosting options and per-token price. Moonshot’s [API documentation](https://platform.kimi.ai/docs/guide/kimi-k3-1-pro-quickstart) already covers Kimi K3.1 Pro, a newer flagship whose full weights Moonshot reportedly promised by November 4, so the field is still moving as of November 3, 2026. The practical question for most teams is whether to call a vendor API, rent a third-party host or run the weights on their own hardware. The answer depends less on a leaderboard score than on three things: what the licence allows, where your data may travel, and what a million tokens costs. A model that wins a coding index but forbids resale as a hosted service is the wrong tool for a platform company, however good it looks on paper. For a pure quality ranking, the [October ranking of open-source LLMs](https://shattered.io/best-open-source-llm-october-2026-kimi-glm-deepseek/) covers the capability side. The deployment and terms side matters more once a pilot turns into a product, and it is where most of the expensive surprises hide. Every figure below comes from vendor pages fetched on November 3 or from clearly labelled third-party listings. Where a number conflicts across sources, the more conservative one wins, and where a claim rests on a single report, the text says so. ![shattered.io](https://shattered.io/static/favicon.svg)· Google · Preferred Sources Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. The scheme targets startups founded within the past five years that have raised less than USD $15 million. Participants will receive 12 months of free access to Firefly Pro Plus, Acrobat Studio, which includes Adobe Express Premium, and Semrush. Adobe is positioning the offer around branding, content creation and customer acquisition at a stage when founders are often handling design, marketing and sales themselves. Alongside software access, the programme includes workshops and other opportunities to learn from Adobe specialists and connect with other founders. **What is included** Firefly Pro Plus is Adobe's generative AI product for image, video and audio work. Acrobat Studio combines PDF tools, Adobe's AI Assistant and Adobe Express, while Semrush adds search and marketing data intended to show how a business appears online across both conventional and AI-led search. The package is designed to bring together content creation, document tools and marketing support in one programme for small teams. Adobe serves a wide range of customers, from individual creators and small businesses to large corporate users. The launch comes as software groups seek to embed AI more deeply into products aimed at smaller businesses and startup teams, which often work with limited budgets and staff. For early-stage companies, branding and customer communication can be difficult to prioritise when product development and fundraising take precedence. **Startup examples** Adobe highlighted several startup users as examples of the businesses it wants to reach through the programme. DataCurve, which works on fan identity and intelligence for sports, media and entertainment organisations, already uses Firefly for creative work and sees broader potential for Adobe tools in linking customer data with content creation. "Creativity is far more powerful when you understand who you're creating for. We already use Adobe Firefly for creative assets, and we see an even bigger opportunity to bring DataCurve's fan intelligence directly into the creative process. AI Product.content: [Skip to main content](#main-content) [Subscribe](/newsletter) # Estée Lauder broadens Microsoft AI partnership The companies are working together to develop solutions for Estée Lauder’s more than 20 beauty brands, including an internal-facing generative AI chatbot and product development tools. By Dan Berthiaume 11/2/2026 ![Stuttgart, Germany - 07-01-2023: Person holding smartphone with logo of US company The Estee Lauder Companies Inc. on screen in front of website. Focus on phone display. Unmodified photo.; Shutterstock ID 2331070563](https://drugstorenews.com/images/v/max_width_640/assetbank_2331070563_0.jpg) Estée Lauder is building on an existing artificial intelligence collaboration with Microsoft to connect its data across all brands, regions and channels. AI Product.content: # Nine Bay Area Venture Capital Firms Launch New Funds in October, Targeting AI, Robotics and Deep Tech ![](https://www.citybiz.co/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/Bay-Area-VC-Firms-Launch-New-Funds.png) Venture capital firms in the San Francisco Bay Area raised millions of dollars in new capital in October 2026, *according to* [*Ivelina Dineva*](https://lnkd.in/p/gD9u-6ne)*, founder of* [*EverythingStartups*](https://www.linkedin.com/company/everythingstartups/home/), reflecting investor interest in artificial intelligence, enterprise software, robotics, deep technology and global startup markets. Nine firms, including Bison Ventures, Endeavor Catalyst, Anorak Ventures and Headline, announced new funds or fundraising milestones during the period, with vehicles ranging from $11.3 million to $400 million. Their investment strategies reveal a venture market increasingly focused on backing AI-driven businesses, developing physical-world technologies and helping early-stage companies turn technical innovation into commercially viable enterprises. ![](https://www.citybiz.co/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/Ivelina-Dineva.png) ###### Founder ### Ivelina Dineva [Connect »](https://www.linkedin.com/in/ivelina-dineva-nft/) ###### Company ### EverythingStartups [Learn More »](https://www.everythingstartups.com/) **Here is a snapshot of the nine firms**: [**49 Palms Ventures**](https://www.linkedin.com/company/49palmsvc/home/)**: A $100 Million Fund Focused on AI Startups and Monetization** PALO ALTO, CALIFORNIA 49 Palms Ventures is building its investment strategy around a problem that is becoming increasingly important for artificial intelligence startups: turning technical capabilities into sustainable revenue. The firm invests in early-stage AI companies and combines capital with advice on pricing, commercial contracts and enterprise sales. Its approach reflects the challenges facing AI founders as they move beyond initial product demonstrations and attempt to establish recurring, economically viable businesses. Founded by [Madhavan Ramanujam](https://www.linkedin.com/in/madhavansf/) and [Josh Bloom](https://www.linkedin.com/in/jbloom49/), the firm draws on the founders’ experience advising companies on pricing and monetization. Their investment thesis centers on helping startups establish commercial models early, including usage-based, outcome-based and hybrid pricing structures. As AI companies face questions about inference costs, including customer acquisition, and the economics of delivering increasingly sophisticated services, the firm’s investment thesis shows that a product that attracts early enterprise interest may still struggle to generate attractive margins if its pricing does not account for infrastructure and deployment costs. 49 Palms says its team has worked with more than 500 companies and 100 unicorns as an investor and adviser to AI founders, with a focus on commercial strategy alongside financing. The firm prioritizes monetization. For founders developing AI applications, enterprise software and infrastructure, that expertise could help bridge the gap between product development and commercial adoption. Dell and NVIDIA are powering the AI revolution, and CrowdStrike is securing it. Together, we're making Falcon's AI-native protection foundational to the AI Factory, giving enterprises the confidence to safely innovate at scale on validated, optimised architectures," said Kurtz. Michael Dell, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of Dell Technologies, said customers want to adopt AI quickly without increasing risk. "Enterprises are under real pressure to move fast on AI, but speed without security creates risk, not value. The Dell AI Factory with NVIDIA gives customers a validated, optimised foundation, and with CrowdStrike's AI-native security integrated from the start, they can move forward with confidence. That's how you give organisations a clear, trusted path from AI ambition to AI out...

Open Source AI.content: ![Georgia Institute of Technology](/legacy/image.php?image=https://media.newswise.com/institutions/7008/GTOneLine_TechGold20211012131057.png) # Researchers Create Tool to Detect AI-Hallucinated Legal Citations 2-Nov-2026 at 10:50 AM EST, by [Georgia Institute of Technology](/institutions/newsroom/7008/) [*♡*](/users/login/?ret=%2Farticles%2Fresearchers-create-tool-to-detect-ai-hallucinated-legal-citations%2F%3Fad2f%3D1%26aid%3D857755 "Add to Favorites") [![Newswise: Researchers Create Tool to Detect AI-Hallucinated Legal Citations](/legacy/image.php?image=aHR0cHM6Ly9uZXdzLnJlc2VhcmNoLmdhdGVjaC5lZHUvc2l0ZXMvZGVmYXVsdC9maWxlcy9zdHlsZXMvd2lkZS9wdWJsaWMvbmV3cy8yMDI2LTEwL0Fkb2JlU3RvY2tfMmNjMGRhZTUtYTkzYy00MmIyLWJmMzAtNDE5MTY2YWE4ZjBiLmpwZy53ZWJwP2l0b2s9M200MFltY3o=)](/articles/media-article/857755 "View full image") Newswise — As more legal documents are drafted with large language models (LLMs), falsified citations are becoming a problem for the people who rely on them. Georgia Tech researchers have created a tool to help lawyers verify their work. Through a donation from IBM, Georgia Tech’s Center for Scientific Software Engineering (CSSE) and Open Source Program Office (OSPO) held a fellowship competition for students to work with mentors at CSSE and OSPO to create the tool. Master’s students [**Adrian Lozada**](https://adrian123l.github.io/) and [**Di Wu**](https://woodygoodenough.com/) were selected as fellows to work on the project. [The Mellea Legal Requirements Checker](https://github.com/gt-csse/mellea-lrc/) (Mellea-LRC) can quickly identify and accurately verify case law citations, specifically checking for citations that are hallucinated by artificial intelligence (AI). One fellowship goal was to give lawyers and others in the legal field a tool to easily verify legal citations. Mella-LRC does this by using both LLMs and IBM’s Mellea open-source framework to verify and repair LLM prompts. The team tested the tool on 26 public court-filing documents containing falsified citations. Mellea-LRC can process a document in about eight minutes. The tool first extracts the case law citations from the legal document. It then verifies that each citation is authentic and supports the document's content. “IBM’s Mellea framework was the foundation we built it on. Mellea’s job is to make model calls predictable: you write the rules the output must satisfy as ordinary code, and the framework retries until LLM output meets them. Our job was to leverage the framework to build the legal application from end to end,” Wu said. An important aspect of the project was ensuring the tool’s code was open source. The team supported this goal by also creating and releasing a new test and validation dataset on Hugging Face – a popular open-source AI development community – for future benchmarking studies. “Agentic AI is growing quickly, and much of the growth happens in open-source projects, where anyone can read, use, and improve the work,” Lozada said. OSPO Director and Principal Research Scientist [**Jeff** **Young**](https://jyoung3131.github.io/) noted that IBM’s Mellea framework was critical to this work in that its “instruct, verify, repair” paradigm allows for the creation of reliable LLM loops as well as the use of small language models (SLMs), such as IBM’s Granite, which can be run on a laptop. “This project demonstrates the power of open-source models like IBM Granite as well as the importance of using novel software engineering and algorithmic techniques from the Mellea project to improve the reliability of our existing LLMs and SLMs. “Mellea-LRC provides a compelling example of AI’s potential to evolve from a source of error in the legal profession into a trusted ally by helping lawyers work faster and cite precedents more accurately,” Young said. **Original release:** <https://news.research.gatech.edu/2026/10/30/researchers-create-tool-detect-ai-hallucinated-legal-citations> [Request an Expert](/resources/expert-query?article_id=857755...

Increasingly, open-source public code is paving the way for that. Public code is a record anyone can read and inspect, and hiring teams are actively using it to assess one's real-world engineering skills. It includes open-source contributions, public repositories (like GitHub), and code samples that hiring managers can evaluate. This is how Uzair Ali landed internships at various global companies and eventually became a founding engineer at a US-based fintech startup. As a college student at the Kalinga Institute of Industrial Technology in Bhubaneswar, Ali was building a tool to monitor server logs. He shared his repository of work in open source on X, which caught the attention of the CTO of Dukaan, an Indian mobile-first, do-it-yourself ecommerce platform**,** leading to an interview at the firm. Ali joined Dukaan as a backend intern in January 2022 in Bengaluru. This was an early lesson in the value of making his work visible to the world. It helped his project reach someone who might otherwise have not seen his resume. Ali's career path did not follow a straight line through a typical hiring funnel at big tech companies. After a stint at Dukaan, he interned at HackerRank and FamPay while still being in university. After graduating, he joined Civo, a London-based cloud infrastructure provider. Twenty-four-year-old Ali is now an engineer at Flip Laboratories, a San Francisco-based fintech startup. He works from India. In an interaction with *YourStory*, Ali says all his career moves from being a backend engineer to AI work and now to being part of the founding team at Flip are largely thanks to his open-source contributions. Ali reasons that open-source code helps software maintainers see how people works over months, while the reviews show how they handle feedback. Now anyone with an internet connection can pick a project, fix what is broken, and receive feedback and reviews. Over time, this history builds a credible repository of one's work in a way a resume cannot, says the techie. Ali's GitHub profile has a number of pull requests merged in various open source projects such as LiteLLM, a widely used open-source LLM gateway. A pull request is a request from others to merge a code into their projects, and this is reveiwed jointly by those who create the code and those who would like to integrate it. Ali's most visible work is on Agno, an open-source framework for building AI agents. It has more than 42,000 stars on GitHub. He also has contributions in major codebases including Terraform, Crossplane, and IntelOwl. In this environment, access to GPUs alone is no longer sufficient. The more difficult task is turning available computing capacity into reliable, cost-efficient token output at scale. Doing so requires not only advanced hardware and software optimization, but also the infrastructure partnerships, operational expertise, and commercial relationships needed to support growing demand. This is the challenge that [TokenPulse](http://www.tokenpulse.com/), a next-generation AI inference infrastructure company headquartered in San Francisco and Singapore, is seeking to address. Following the opening of its Asia-Pacific Operating Hub in Singapore, the company is bringing together data-center resources, GPU infrastructure, optimized inference engines, and globally coordinated serving capabilities to support AI workloads across regions. Beyond its technology strategy, TokenPulse is placing considerable emphasis on the leadership team responsible for putting that infrastructure into operation. With backgrounds spanning data centers, government, investment, cloud engineering, and enterprise commercialization, its executives bring different capabilities to the increasingly complex business of AI inference. ## Infrastructure Leadership and Regional Delivery At the center of TokenPulse’s infrastructure strategy is Chairman Thomas Pang, whose more than 30 years of executive experience span government, investment, infrastructure, and corporate leadership. Pang spent over two decades with Keppel, including serving as CEO of Keppel’s Data Centres & Networks Division from 2014 to 2024. In that role, he oversaw the group’s global data-center portfolio and digital connectivity businesses, gaining experience in the infrastructure development and partnerships that underpin large-scale computing operations. That background is particularly relevant as TokenPulse expands its presence in Southeast Asia. While GPU performance and software efficiency remain central to AI inference, the ability to secure suitable data-center capacity, coordinate regional infrastructure resources, and establish long-term partnerships can be equally important to commercial delivery. From its Singapore operating hub, TokenPulse is developing infrastructure relationships across Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand, and the wider region. Logo, The Next Platform](/view-resources/dachser2/public/nextplatform/logo-white.svg)](https://www.nextplatform.com) NEXTPLATFORM AD # Qualcomm Has Eyes On The AI Inference Datacenter With HBC And AI250 Jeff Burt [Jeff Burt](https://www.nextplatform.com/author/Jeff-Burt) Published ### READ MORE * [#### Marvell wants to be a copper topper, bets $115B on photonics leader to push optical networking](/systems/2026/11/02/marvell-wants-to-be-a-copper-topper-bets-115b-on-photonics-leader-to-push-optical-networking/5307028) * [#### Oracle gobbles $20 billion borrowing limit a week after setting it](/paas-and-iaas/2026/11/02/oracle-gobbles-20-billion-borrowing-limit-a-week-after-setting-it/5307014) * [#### Ericsson says it can detect, track drones using only mobile networks](/networks/2026/11/02/ericsson-says-it-can-detect-track-drones-using-only-mobile-networks/5306958) * [#### Thieves pilfer environment variables from Trigger AI workflow tool](/security/2026/11/02/thieves-pilfer-environment-variables-from-trigger-ai-workflow-tool/5306998) * [#### Token thieves costing companies $100K+ per day in illicit LLM charges](/security/2026/11/02/token-thieves-costing-companies-100k-per-day-in-illicit-llm-charges/5306967) Qualcomm executives this summer [introduced an architecture](https://www.qualcomm.com/news/onq/2026/07/qualcomm-hbc-near-memory-computing) called high-bandwidth computing (HBC), the solution to an ongoing problem in AI inferencing – [and now in agentic AI](https://www.nextplatform.com/compute/2026/10/29/sponsored-how-to-evaluate-cpu-performance-for-agentic-ai/5305779) – that they and others call [the memory wall](https://www.nextplatform.com/store/2026/09/16/how-to-smash-the-memory-wall-plaguing-high-performance-systems/5296866). Essentially, the performance of these models increasingly depends less on the compute capability of a processor – how fast the chip can calculate – and more on how quickly the chip can feed data to the calculation. It’s an issue that affects both the performance of the AI model as well as the cost for running the AI workloads. Qualcomm outlined two strategies that are widely used – one that houses the AI model in fast on-chip memory, and another that uses stacked high-bandwidth memory (HBM) to support a processor. Qualcomm advocates a third strategy – near-memory computing, or HBC – that moves the computer closers to [the all-important memory](https://www.nextplatform.com/store/2026/10/08/memory-is-the-lynchpin-of-the-it-industry-and-doubly-so-for-ai/5301841). NEXTPLATFORM AD Executives argue that to close a widening gap – to remove the memory wall – between the need for more compute and the ability to feed that demand with data, the compute needs to move closer to the memory and the data it holds. It gives the AI model faster access to the data it needs, and reduces the time, energy, and cost that come when the data needs to travel a longer distance to get to the compute. It’s an argument Qualcomm made in July when first pitching the HBC architecture, and one they continue to make now. “In traditional computer architecture, you usually have DDR, you have memory of package, you have usually plenty of capacity on that, but you have a narrow link, which moves the data very slowly,” Gerardo Giaretta, vice president and general manager of datacenter CPU and AI at Qualcomm, recently told journalists and analysts. “So far, AI has been really focusing on the HBM architecture. It basically increases the number of lanes and how fast you can move the data between the compute and the HBM. Infra & Chips.content: # From capacity, to the cost of intelligence Amit Agrawal, President, Techno Digital The next shift in AI infrastructure We are already in an era where intelligence comes with a price tag. Every answer, inference, agent, and AI workflow carries a real infrastructure cost, and that cost isn't determined by the model alone. It rises or falls with compute efficiency, utilization, power, cooling, networking, latency, and workload architecture. The same intelligence can have radically different economics depending on where, when, and how it is delivered. Back in March 2023, running a GPT-4-class model cost roughly $20 per million tokens. Today, that same intelligence costs less than $0.50, a fall of nearly 98 percent in three years. Yet the average enterprise AI budget has grown nearly six times over the same period, from $1.2 million in 2024 to approximately $7 million in 2026. Intelligence has never been cheaper. AI has never cost more. Unit price is falling while total spend rises. That is the paradox defining AI infrastructure in 2026, and it is why the industry’s most important conversation is shifting from how much capacity we can build to how much usable intelligence that capacity can deliver, per dollar, per watt, and per second. What follows is the case for that shift: the economics behind it, the chips accelerating it, and the power constraint quietly capping it. ## From capacity to productivity The first phase of the AI infrastructure race was necessarily about capacity. Compute was scarce, demand was accelerating, and hyperscalers, enterprises, and governments moved quickly to secure GPUs, power, and data center capacity. That capacity remains essential, but it doesn't by itself determine AI economics. A GPU cluster running at high utilization has very different unit economics from the same cluster sitting partially idle. The question is evolving from how much compute is available to how productively that compute converts into usable intelligence. Earlier this year, a widely circulated figure claimed DeepSeek had trained a frontier model for just $5.6 million. That number actually referred to pre-training compute for an earlier model, not the total cost of the frontier model itself, a distinction lost in the headlines. Weeks later, Microsoft, Meta, Amazon, and Google all reaffirmed or increased their AI capex guidance rather than cutting it. This is Jevons’ paradox in action: when efficiency gains lower the price of a resource, total consumption tends to rise, not fall. Every dollar saved per token becomes the reason to run ten more tokens in parallel, not the reason to build less. ## The price of a GPU is not the cost of intelligence Nvidia’s own Blackwell-vs-Hopper analysis illustrates the distinction. While newer-generation infrastructure can carry a higher GPU-hour cost, its delivered cost per million tokens can be substantially lower because of gains in throughput, memory, interconnect, software optimization, and energy efficiency. Buyers evaluating AI infrastructure on hardware price or theoretical compute performance alone are therefore optimizing for an incomplete metric. The true cost of intelligence is determined by the entire stack. Model efficiency determines how much computation an output requires. Compute architecture determines how efficiently accelerators, memory, and interconnects execute the workload. Utilization determines how much installed infrastructure is doing productive work rather than sitting idle. Infrastructure efficiency determines how effectively power and cooling support high-density compute. And workload placement determines the latency, network, and data-movement economics of where intelligence is produced and consumed. Optimizing any one layer in isolation can produce misleading economics. A highly efficient model running on poorly utilized infrastructure can still be expensive. Infra & Chips.title: Nebul deploys Nvidia GPUs at Datacenter United campus in Belgium - DCD
Infra & Chips.titleZh: Nebul deploys Nvidia GPUs at Datacenter United campus in Belgium - DCD
Infra & Chips.content: # Nebul deploys Nvidia GPUs at Datacenter United campus in Belgium European AI cloud leasing capacity in Machelen European AI cloud provider Nebul is expanding its footprint into Belgium. The company has contracted its second data center location, at Datacenter United's campus in Machelen, Belgium. The site will host a new ‘SuperCluster’ comprised of more than 1,000 liquid-cooled Nvidia Blackwell Ultra GPUs in GB300 NVL72 systems, to be supplied by Lenovo. “This is a defining moment for Europe’s ambitions in AI,” said Arnold Juffer, CEO of Nebul. “Organizations want to amplify what they can achieve without giving up control over the intelligence they build. The demand is there, and it is larger than the capacity Europe is building today. With more than 1,000 Nvidia Blackwell Ultra GPUs as a part of GB300 NVL72 rack-scale systems in Belgium, and Datacenter United, Lenovo and Nvidia as partners, we are delivering on that demand. And this Belgium deployment is a next step.” Nebul is a European private AI cloud provider based in Leiden, South Holland. Via its AI cloud, Nebul offers Nvidia platforms, including DGX, HGX, OVX, and RTX, with GPUs including B300, B200, H200, H100, L40S, and L4. The neocloud raised €20 million ($22.7m) in a June 2024 funding round. Earlier this year, the firm announced it would be the first cloud platform to offer Speedata's Analytics Processing Units (APUs). Datacenter United, founded in 2010, currently operates 14 data centers across 12 locations in Belgium. TINC acquired a 75 percent equity interest in Datacenter United in 2020, with Cordiant (since rebranded Corilis) taking a stake in the firm in 2024. “Europe’s AI ambitions depend on more than computing power alone. They require reliable, high-density infrastructure that can support the next generation of AI workloads,” said Friso Haringsma, CEO of Datacenter United. “Nebul’s decision to establish its new SuperCluster in Machelen demonstrates that Belgium has a meaningful role to play in Europe’s AI development. By providing the power, connectivity and advanced liquid-cooling infrastructure required for this deployment, we are helping turn those ambitions into reality.”

PRESS RELEASE — FuriosaAI, an AI semiconductor company building sustainable, high-performance inference compute for data centers, announced the completion of its $620 million (KRW 820 billion) Series D round, bringing its post-money valuation to approximately $2.9 billion. The financing marks a major milestone as FuriosaAI scales global commercial deployments of its RNGD AI inference accelerator. FuriosaAI will use the new capital to expand RNGD production, strengthen its software ecosystem, and accelerate development of its third-generation AI accelerator. International investors contributed a total of $110 million to the round, bringing deep expertise across AI semiconductors and computing infrastructure. U.S.-based Infinitum, an investment firm with extensive experience in the AI semiconductor sector, was the largest international investor in the round. Singapore-based QUDA Capital Partners also joined the round. Other international investors include Cisco Investments, Abu Dhabi-based NeoFort Holding, and U.S.-based technology investment firms Jericho Capital and Worldline Capital. South Korea’s National Growth Fund invested $280 million as the largest investor in the round, supporting the country’s initiatives to expand AI computing infrastructure and strengthen the Korean AI semiconductor ecosystem, while helping accelerate the round’s momentum.
